source.title_on_document: Harnessing generative AI for collaborative creativity: A study of university students’ engagement and innovation

paper_design_summary: Fifty undergraduate English majors enrolled in a Communication Skills course were randomly divided into AI-supported and non-AI conditions of 25 students for a collaborative cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1-3.2.2). Students in the AI condition prompted ChatGPT-3 during ideation; two trained raters scored fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, and post-task reflections were analyzed separately as qualitative data (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.2-3.2.4). The paper reports 25 analyzed students per arm, but does not explain individual scoring of collaborative outputs or establish whether the task was ordinary coursework or a separate supervised research session (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.1-3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly divided between a non-AI control condition and an AI-supported experimental condition, with 25 students per condition. Recruitment into the study was purposive; assignment to conditions is explicitly described as random. The randomization procedure is not specified.
assignment.quote: The students were then randomly divided into two groups of 25: one group performed the task without AI assistance (control group), while the other used AI (experimental group).

arms.name: Non-AI control
arms.description: Completed the cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task without AI, working face-to-face and recording responses on paper or a shared Google document (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1). The assignment count is given in section 3.1; the analysis count is given on PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

arms.name: AI-supported (ChatGPT-3)
arms.description: Received training in ChatGPT-3 and used specific inquiries to generate and develop concepts during the identical Alternative Uses Task; instructed to distinguish AI-generated and human-written material (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2). The assignment count is given in section 3.1; the analysis count is given on PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

participants.exclusions: Exclusions and attrition are not reported. Section 3.1 describes 50 students randomly divided into groups of 25; section 4.1 reports n = 25 in each analyzed arm (PDF pp. 4-5).
participants.who: Undergraduate English majors enrolled in the Communication Skills course at the National University of Modern Languages (NUML), Islamabad, during spring 2024; 25 male and 25 female students, aged 18-22 years, recruited purposively from the same course (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).
participants.quote: An independent-samples t-test was used to assess differences in creative output between the two groups: the AI-assisted experimental group (n = 25) and the non-AI control group (n = 25).
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (journal p. 3287), section 3.1, for recruitment, demographics and randomized counts; PDF p. 5 (journal p. 3288), section 4.1, for analyzed arm counts; PDF p. 1, author affiliation 1, identifies NUML Islamabad as Pakistan.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-3 (the paper’s name; exact underlying model/version not specified)
ai_tool.how_used: Students received ChatGPT-3 training before the task, then directed the chatbot through specific inquiries to generate and develop concepts during the collaborative AUT. They were instructed to distinguish AI-generated and human-written contributions. Exact prompts, chat logs, access configuration, underlying model version, and training duration are not reported (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; PDF p. 5, section 4.1).

task.description: Collaboratively generate multiple and varied uses for a cardboard box in the Alternative Uses Task. The control-condition description specifies face-to-face work and responses recorded on paper or a shared Google document; the AI arm completed the identical AUT with ChatGPT-3 (PDF p. 4, sections 3.2.1-3.2.2). Subsequent reflective writing supplied qualitative accounts of the experience and was not scored for creative performance (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.2.1-3.2.4).
task.duration: 10 minutes for collaborative idea generation, stated for each group in section 3.2.1; section 3.2.2 calls the AI task identical (PDF p. 4, journal p. 3287).

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Task: fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct AUT ideas generated (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2.3). Two trained raters independently scored the ideas using an adapted creativity rubric; their domain expertise, blinding, aggregation rules, and numerical inter-rater reliability are not supplied (PDF p. 5, section 3.2.2.3). Participant records the apparent unit of the reported analysis: section 4.1 gives n = 25 students per arm and Table 1 gives t(48); section 4.4 describes participant scores. However, the methods describe collaborative group output and do not explain individual-score construction, the number of independent teams or output records, or adjustment for dependence within groups (PDF pp. 4-6, sections 3.2.1, 4.1 and 4.4, Table 1). Figure 1 presents the same four dimensions; its accompanying text identifies the error bars as standard deviations (PDF p. 6, journal p. 3289).

eligibility.reason: All three core criteria are met on the paper's explicit reporting for S1. Students were randomly divided into AI and non-AI conditions (PDF p. 4, section 3.1), and the quantitative analysis reports 25 analyzed students per arm, meeting the 50-person threshold exactly (PDF p. 5, section 4.1). Trained raters scored four creativity dimensions on the AUT outputs, with ChatGPT-3 available to the experimental arm during production (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.2-3.2.2.3 and 4.1, Table 1). The unresolved lab-versus-field setting leaves design_class null but does not negate random assignment. Collaborative production versus apparent participant-level analysis requires clarification of independent units and precision before pooling. The Figure 2 discussion refers inconsistently to fifty AI users (PDF p. 7, section 4.6); it supplies no revised allocation or quantitative sample and does not overturn the explicit methods and quantitative comparison. Authors should clarify the reflection denominator and timing of any additional AI exposure; this could affect criterion 1 if controls used AI during the scored AUT.

one_line_finding: Among 50 analyzed students, the AI-supported arm scored higher than the no-AI arm on fluency (22.8 vs. 15.2), flexibility (11.6 vs. 8.4), originality (7.9 vs. 6.1), and elaboration (24.5 vs. 18.3; PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1).
open_questions: Was the AUT part of ordinary coursework or a separate supervised research session? The paper establishes course enrollment and face-to-face group work, but does not distinguish these settings. Neither lab_rct nor field_rct is confirmed; design_class is null (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1-3.2.2).

How were individual creativity scores constructed from collaborative responses, how many independent teams or output records existed, and how was within-group dependence handled? The task describes groups of 25, whereas the tests use n = 25 per arm and t(48) (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

What were the full scoring rubric, category scheme, rating scales, score aggregation rules, originality normative sample, rater qualifications and blinding, and numerical inter-rater reliability? The paper says Cohen’s kappa was calculated but supplies no value (PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.2.2.3).

Why does the text below Figure 2 describe fifty students who implemented ChatGPT-3 when the quantitative experiment assigns only 25 to AI? The reflection denominator and any additional AI exposure are unspecified; quantitative counts are taken from section 4.1 (PDF p. 7, Figure 2 discussion; PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.1 and 4.1).
Which exact model and deployment does ChatGPT-3 identify, and what training and prompt instructions were used beyond the brief description? These details are not supplied (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2).
notes: Both raw forms parsed successfully. Read every line of the markdown conversion, including the final references; checked PDF pages 1, 4-8 and 11-13, and extracted Table 1 with PyMuPDF find_tables. Locators use one-based PDF pages; printed journal pages run from 3284 to 3296. The only substantive disagreement between the forms is lab_rct versus field_rct. Compared assignment, matched arms by name despite reversed ordering, participant counts, AI tool and role, task, the four outcome lists and every coding field, all reported statistics and locators, supplement, sample overlap, company involvement, eligibility criteria, and finding. Different wording, expanded caveats, and additional corroborating locators do not change the underlying values and are not counted as separate differences. B's additional Figure 1 description and result-section locators were checked against the PDF and retained; they refer to the same four outcomes and statistics, not additional outcomes. The unresolved setting disagreement is recorded as null rather than guessing one randomized subtype; the randomized between-person design itself is explicit. The participant outcome unit records the paper's apparent analysis, not verified independent individual production. The qualitative reflection themes concerning apprehension, fixation, and role ambiguity are subjective accounts, not creativity or between-person diversity scored on output; they therefore supply neither across_people nor after_ai outcomes (PDF pp. 4-5, qualitative methods; PDF pp. 6-8, sections 4.6-4.9). All four eligible outcomes answer with_ai and concern the immediate AUT; no primary outcome, preregistration, supplement, public data/code link, or shared-sample disclosure is stated. The PDF ends with References, with no appended supplement. Unknown external supplement locations, overlap, and data/code URLs are null. Negative t-statistics are preserved as printed, while treatment_higher reflects the higher AI-arm means. No effect sizes or other unprinted statistics were calculated. n_unresolved counts unresolved A/B differences; shared reporting limitations are retained in open_questions. Final review: read the complete markdown conversion, lines 1-495 through the final reference, and extracted PDF text on pages 1, 4-8, 11 and 13. Rechecked every recorded outcome mean, SD, t-statistic and p-value against PDF p. 5, Table 1 using PyMuPDF find_tables, and checked randomized/analyzed counts, demographics, task duration, raters and source metadata against PDF pp. 1 and 4-6. All three challenge files (assignment, outcome and people) contain empty problems arrays, so challenge_resolution is empty and all challenge-resolution counters are zero; their confirmations were independently checked. Existing source.supplement coding remains supported: no supplement is identified or appended. This is an original experiment, so the reanalysis design rule does not apply. Counts at analysis are described as analyzed; assignment counts are explicitly supported. All five open_questions and the unresolved design_class reconciliation difference are addressed in final.open_items. The possible control-group AI-exposure issue is flagged as potentially affecting criterion 1 without replacing the explicit quantitative design with an inferred one. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

open_items.item: Study setting (open_questions[0] and the unresolved reconciliation.differences[0]): whether the AUT was ordinary coursework or a separate supervised research session. Author confirmation would settle lab_rct versus field_rct; both are randomized designs, so this does not affect any eligibility criterion. Course enrollment and face-to-face work alone do not settle the distinction (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1-3.2.2).

Individual-score construction and independent observations (open_questions[1]): authors must explain how collaborative responses yielded participant scores, identify independent teams/output records, and describe any adjustment for within-group dependence (PDF pp. 4-6, sections 3.2.1, 4.1 and 4.4, Table 1). This affects precision and pooling, not the three eligibility criteria: the source explicitly reports random allocation, 50 analyzed people and scored AUT outputs.

Scoring documentation (open_questions[2]): authors must supply the full rubric, category scheme, rating scales, aggregation rules, originality normative sample, rater qualifications/blinding and numerical inter-rater reliability. The paper describes two trained raters and calculation of Cohen's kappa without its value (PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.2.2.3). These gaps affect measurement assessment and reproducibility; criterion 3 is already met by explicit scoring of AUT outputs. No supplement or public data location is stated.

Reflection denominator and timing of any control-group AI exposure (open_questions[3]): the text below Figure 2 calls fifty students ChatGPT-3 users, whereas the methods and quantitative results specify 25 AI students and 25 controls (PDF p. 7, section 4.6; PDF p. 4, section 3.1; PDF p. 5, section 4.1). Authors must clarify whether this is a description/denominator error or whether additional AI use occurred, and whether that use preceded or followed the scored AUT. This could affect criterion 1 if it changes the reported AI-versus-no-AI contrast during production; the explicit randomized quantitative comparison remains the basis for the current met judgment.

Exact ChatGPT-3 model/deployment, training and prompt instructions (open_questions[4]): authors must identify the deployed model and supply the intervention instructions beyond the brief methods description (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2). These details affect reproducibility, not eligibility: the paper explicitly describes a content-generating chatbot used during the AUT.
